title: Given an array sorted in non-decreasing order that may contain negative numbers, return a new array of the squares of each number, also sorted in non-decreasing order. Aim for linear time. (LeetCode: Squares of a Sorted Array)
shortTitle: Squaring a Sorted Array (Two Pointers from the Ends)

s1_definition.profdef: Squaring a sorted array that contains negatives produces squares whose largest values come from the two ends of the array, because a large negative squared can exceed a small positive squared. The linear solution uses two pointers at the ends, compares the absolute values, squares the larger, and places it at the end of the result array, filling the result from back to front. This achieves linear time without sorting the squares again.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh has a sorted list of daily profit-and-loss figures, where losses are negative and profits are positive. He wants the squared magnitudes sorted smallest to largest. The catch is that a big loss squared can be larger than a small profit squared, so the biggest squared magnitudes live at the two ends of the sorted list. Priya reads from both ends inward, each time taking whichever end has the bigger magnitude, squaring it, and dropping it into the back of a new tray, filling the tray from the last slot to the first.
s1_definition.oneliner: The largest squares hide at the ends, so compare the two ends, square the bigger, and fill the result from the back.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Squaring a sorted array that contains negatives produces squares whose largest values come from the two ends of the array, because a large negative squared can exceed a small positive squared. The linear solution uses two pointers at the ends, compares the absolute values, squares the larger, and places it at the end of the result array, filling the result from back to front. This achieves linear time without sorting the squares again.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine Rajesh has a sorted list of daily profit-and-loss figures, where losses are negative and profits are positive. He wants the squared magnitudes sorted smallest to largest. The catch is that a big loss squared can be larger than a small profit squared, so the biggest squared magnitudes live at the two ends of the sorted list. Priya reads from both ends inward, each time taking whichever end has the bigger magnitude, squaring it, and dropping it into the back of a new tray, filling the tray from the last slot to the first.

**One line to remember:** The largest squares hide at the ends, so compare the two ends, square the bigger, and fill the result from the back.

sections.s2_technical:
If the array had only non-negative numbers, squaring would preserve the order and we could square each element left to right. The complication is negative numbers: because the array is sorted, the most negative value sits at the far left, and its square can be the largest value of all. So the smallest square is somewhere in the middle, and the largest squares are at the two ends.

The efficient trick is to build the result from the largest square down to the smallest. We place a `left` pointer at index 0 and a `right` pointer at the last index, and a `position` pointer at the last index of a new result array. At each step we compare the absolute values of `arr[left]` and `arr[right]`. Whichever has the larger magnitude produces the larger square, so we square it, store it at `result[position]`, move that end pointer inward, and decrement `position`. We repeat until the two pointers cross.

A finance usage example: suppose daily P&L figures sorted are `[-7, -3, 2, 5, 8]`. The squares are 49, 9, 4, 25, 64. We want `[4, 9, 25, 49, 64]`. Starting, `left` points at -7 (magnitude 7) and `right` at 8 (magnitude 8). Eight is larger, so 64 goes into the last result slot and `right` moves to 5. Now -7 magnitude 7 versus 5 magnitude 5, so 49 goes into the next slot from the back and `left` moves to -3. Continuing this way fills the result in descending square order from the back, producing the sorted output.

The senior-level nuance: filling from the back is what makes this linear. A naive approach would square every element then sort, costing `n log n`. The two-pointer method exploits the existing sort to reach linear time. We compare absolute values rather than raw values because we care about magnitude; comparing with squares directly also works and avoids a sign concern, though for very large values computing the square early can risk overflow, so using a wide enough type or comparing magnitudes first is safer.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India's risk desk keeps a sorted array of a trading book's daily profit-and-loss figures, where losses are negative and profits are positive. To compute a volatility-style measure, the desk needs the squared magnitude of each day's result, and it needs those squares sorted so it can quickly find the median and the extremes. The naive approach of squaring everything and re-sorting is too slow for the millions of figures the desk processes across many books.

Problem 2 — Because a large loss squared can dominate a small profit squared, the desk cannot assume the input order carries over to the squares. The solution must correctly account for negatives while still running in a single linear pass.

The code defines a `PnlSquarer` class with a `sortedSquares` method that takes the sorted P&L array and returns a new sorted array of squares using two end pointers and back-to-front filling. A runnable demo seeds a sorted P&L array including losses and logs the sorted squares.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the sorted P&L array `[-7, -3, 2, 5, 8]`.

Step 1: The squarer creates an empty result array of length 5. It sets `left` to index 0 (value -7), `right` to index 4 (value 8), and `pos` to index 4, the last result slot.

Step 2: It compares squares: left square is 49, right square is 64. The right is larger, so 64 goes into result slot 4. `right` moves to index 3 (value 5) and `pos` becomes 3.

Step 3: Left square is 49, right square is 25. The left is larger, so 49 goes into result slot 3. `left` moves to index 1 (value -3) and `pos` becomes 2.

Step 4: Left square is 9, right square is 25. The right is larger, so 25 goes into result slot 2. `right` moves to index 2 (value 2) and `pos` becomes 1.

Step 5: Left square is 9, right square is 4. The left is larger, so 9 goes into result slot 1. `left` moves to index 2 and `pos` becomes 0. Now `left` equals `right` at value 2.

Step 6: Left square equals right square at 4, so 4 goes into result slot 0 and the pointers cross. The result array is `[4, 9, 25, 49, 64]`, sorted ascending.

Final output:

```
Oct 27, 2026 6:00:00 PM com.bank.risk.PnlSquarerDemo main
INFO: Input P&L: [-7, -3, 2, 5, 8]
INFO: Sorted squares = [4, 9, 25, 49, 64]
INFO: Volatility magnitudes: [4, 9, 25, 49, 64]
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Squaring a sorted array that may contain negative numbers is trickier than it first looks, because a large negative value squared can be bigger than a small positive value squared. That means the largest squared values live at the two ends of the sorted array, and the smallest square is somewhere in the middle. The naive approach of squaring everything and re-sorting costs n-log-n, but I can do it in linear time by exploiting the existing sort order.

I use two pointers, one at each end of the input, and I build the result array from the back toward the front. At each step I compare the magnitudes of the two end values, square whichever is larger, place that square in the next slot from the back of the result, and move that end's pointer inward. I keep doing this until the two pointers cross. Because the largest remaining square is always at one of the two ends, filling the result from the last slot backward produces a fully sorted array in a single linear pass.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this on the risk desk. We kept a trading book's daily profit-and-loss figures in a sorted array, where losses were negative and profits were positive, and the desk needed the squared magnitudes sorted to compute a volatility measure and quickly read off the median and the extremes. With millions of figures across many books, squaring and re-sorting each time was too slow, so the two-pointer linear method kept the computation within our latency budget.

The senior-level point I make is about correctness and overflow. I compare magnitudes rather than raw values because the sign does not matter for the square, and I cast to a wider numeric type before multiplying so that squaring large figures does not overflow. I also note the contrast with the simpler case: if the array had no negatives, squaring preserves order and a plain left-to-right pass would do, but the moment negatives appear, the two-ended fill-from-the-back technique is the right tool, and being able to explain exactly why the largest squares sit at the ends is what demonstrates I understand the structure rather than memorizing steps.
